transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date/Time: 2028-10-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Samir Shah (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Hawthorn CTO), Jonas Li (ML Infra Lead), Rosa Martinez (SRE), Evan Brooks (Product)

Summary:
Brief discovery focused on p95 latency targets, steady-state concurrency expectations, streaming token/sec behaviour, and tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem). Customer interested in fallback strategies for burst events and measurable token/sec benchmarks for production SLAs.

Topics:
- p95 targets and how they map to model choice and batching
- concurrency and burst handling (reserved capacity vs auto-burst)
- streaming vs non-streaming latency characteristics
- token/sec benchmarking approach and what artifacts Redwood can provide
- security/compliance: SOC2, KMS, VPC networking

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Alex, AE on the account. Samir is our SE who will run through the performance questions.
[00:18] Priya (CTO): Hi, Priya here. We're trying to scope either your hosted API or potentially Dedicated or Private. Main concern is p95 under load — our target is around 250-350ms for short responses but for streaming chat flows we need p95 under 800ms.
[00:34] Samir (SE): Got it. Do you have model families you're planning to use? LLMs vary a lot.
[00:42] Jonas (ML Infra): We're mostly on a trimmed set — 7B and 13B distill-ish models for user-facing chat, and larger 70B for internal LLMs. The chat paths are streaming token-by-token.
[00:58] Rosa (SRE): Also want to flag we get bursts — during morning sync windows we see spikes up to 200 concurrent sessions that generate stream traffic. Steady-state is closer to 40-60 concurrent.
[01:16] Alex: Okay that helps. We typically talk about p95 in the context of token latency and end-to-end response. For streaming you'll see two metrics — first byte and per-token p95.
[01:28] Priya: In plain terms, what's realistic on Hosted vs Dedicated? We like hosted for ease but worried about noise and multi-tenant variability.
[01:36] Samir: Short answer: Hosted gets you fast time-to-value; we publish performance profiles for our curated models. Dedicated gives you predictable throughput and burst capacity — you can reserve GPU pools. Private (VPC or on-prem) is for strict isolation and network control.
[01:50] Jonas: Can you share an example? Say 13B streaming at 12 tokens/sec per session — what's p95 token latency?
[01:58] Samir: It depends on token size and model. For a 13B with optimized kernels and continous batching, we often see per-token latency in the 15-40ms range median; p95 can be 60-140ms at reasonable concurrency on Dedicated. Hosted might be slightly higher due to noisy neighbors — maybe add 20-40% on p95 in some regions.
[02:22] Priya: Hmm, that could push us over our 800ms end-to-end if users have long responses.
[02:28] Alex: That's where batching, prefix caching (K V cache), and early-streaming heuristics come in. We can reduce cost and keep p95 low by tuning batch windows and enabling prefix KV cache for repeated prompts.
[02:40] Rosa: You said K V cache? Our docs sometimes show "KV cache" — transcription spelled it out oddly.
[02:46] Samir: Yeah KV cache — apologies, some of our transcripts show it as K V.
[02:49] Evan (Product): On the fallback side, if Dedicated is saturated, what's the transparent behavior? Does request fail or redirect?
[02:58] Samir: We have policy-based routing. Typical setup: primary route to Dedicated, fallback to a lower-cost hosted variant or a quantized model with slightly lower quality. We can also configure automatic queuing, burst capacity, and rate-limited degradation instead of hard failures.
[03:14] Priya: Can you do canary rollouts? We want to test a fallback quantized model with 5% of traffic first.
[03:20] Alex: Yes — rollouts/canaries are supported in the Console. We'll note that as an action item to show the dashboard.
[03:26] Jonas: For benchmarking, we'd like a reproducible script. Does Redwood provide something like a token/sec harness that emulates streaming sessions?
[03:34] Samir: We have a small benchmark harness that simulates streaming sessions, measures per-token p95, throughput (tokens/sec) and end-to-end p95. We'll share a workshop script. It uses a mix of seq lengths and throttled client rates to emulate real user variance.
[03:48] Priya: What's your recommended concurrency config to test our spikes?
[03:52] Samir: I'd run three phases: steady-state at 50 concurrent sessions, medium at 150, and spike at 220-250. Capture per-token p95 and end-to-end p95 for short (8-20 token replies) and long (80-300 token) responses.
[04:08] Priya: Our big worry is that streaming has variable per-token latency: early tokens are fast but later tokens balloon.
[04:14] Samir: That's common. Two causes: KV cache misses and batch window growth. We can instrument to show token latency across sequence position. Also, quantization can change execution patterns — some quantized backends have different tail latencies.
[04:28] Rosa: Any specific network implications for VPC/private? Our security team wants to ensure sub-100ms intra-datacenter latency to GPU hosts.
[04:36] Samir: For Private deployments we provide a customer-managed control plane and we can do an on-prem package. We'll need a network diagram; typically the in-cluster network latency is negligible if done right. Key is egress rules and NAT throughput — we can share our on-prem checklist.
[04:50] Priya: SOC2 and KMS — does Redwood support HSM-backed KMS?
[04:56] Alex: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping; we'll include the SOC2 AOC and guide.
[05:02] Jonas: Cost — what's the delta between Dedicated and Hosted at our scale?
[05:08] Alex: Depends on committed capacity and model. Dedicated is a reservation model — you pay for reserved GPU pools but get lower per-token unit costs. Hosted is pay-as-you-go; sometimes it's cheaper at low volume but less predictable at scale. We'll send a sample cost sheet with assumptions for your workload.
[05:24] Evan: Do you support automatic quantization suggestions per workload?
[05:28] Samir: Yes, our Optimize module recommends quantization and batching profiles based on evals. We'll include recommended profiles for your 13B/70B mix.
[05:36] Priya: About benchmarks — we're expecting you to run a bench on our data or do we run it?
[05:42] Samir: Both options. For Private/pilot we can run in your environment with an SE-assisted run. For Hosted/Dedicated we can run in our infra with representative datasets but results are best in your network.
[05:54] Rosa: If you run it in your infra, how do we know it's representative?
[05:58] Samir: We instrument and share raw logs and p95 traces. We also encourage you to run the harness in your VPC during a scheduled window; we'll support with credentials and scripts.
[06:08] Priya: Any pitfalls? What should we watch for in the RFP?
[06:12] Alex: Common gotchas: not specifying tail p95 targets for streaming, not sharing realistic prompt distributions, and expecting linear scaling for token/sec — there are diminishing returns due to batching inefficiencies.
[06:24] Jonas: Quick technical deep dive — how do you manage KV cache across model variants when fallback happens?
[06:30] Samir: We have cache compatibility layers and prefix normalization. When you fallback to a quantized variant, the kv shapes are compatible for most transformer-based models; we'd verify on model onboarding. There are occasional mismatches with custom tuning layers.
[06:46] Priya: We might want initial pilot on Dedicated with a small reservation and fallback to Hosted. Can you support that hybrid routing policy?
[06:54] Alex: Absolutely — that's a common pattern. We'll outline needed configs in the follow-up doc.
[07:00] Evan: Any limits on streaming sessions per GPU? We want to estimate saturation points.
[07:06] Samir: We size by tokens/sec and concurrency; a single A100-class GPU serving a 13B optimized runner can handle X concurrent streaming sessions at ~Y tokens/sec depending on quantization. We'll provide concrete numbers in the sheet — numbers differ if you use continuous batching aggressively.
[07:22] Priya: Can you share an example of a p95 trace visualization?
[07:26] Samir: Yes, we'll share a dashboard screenshot and a small tracing export. Link: https://redwood.ai/decks/hawthorn-benchmarking (we'll email full versions).
[07:36] Rosa: Regarding SLAs — do you offer latency SLAs or just uptime?
[07:40] Alex: We provide uptime SLAs for Dedicated; latency SLAs are more involved but we offer p95 targets tied to Dedicated plans and committed configs. We'll include a sample SLA clause.
[07:52] Priya: For the pilot, timeline wise we want a pilot in region EU-west early November. Can you support that?
[07:58] Alex: Yes, we can arrange Dedicated reservation and a pilot kickoff the week of Nov 6th.
[08:04] Jonas: One last question — how do you measure and report regression in output quality when doing quantized fallbacks?
[08:10] Samir: We tie quality evals to prompt sets and run A/B regressions. Our Optimize toolkit flags regressions and links them to model/quantization changes. We'll include an example eval report.
[08:22] Priya: Great. That addresses most of our concerns.
[08:26] Alex: Quick recap of next steps: Alex will send latency/cost spreadsheet and the benchmarking harness; Samir will prepare a streaming checklist and sample dashboard screenshots; Priya will share prompt set and concurrency traces. We'll schedule the on-prem pilot scoping for the week of Nov 6th.
[08:44] Priya: Sounds good. Thank you.
[08:46] Alex: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the links and calendar invite.

Questions (recorded):
- How does Dedicated fallback to Hosted behave during sustained bursts?
- What shapes tail p95 for long streaming responses and how to mitigate?
- What deliverables do we get for Private/on-prem pilot (network checklist, KMS steps)?
